body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The tragedy of Percy, the most favourable specimen of Miss Hannah Moore’s poetical talents, was revived at this theatre on Tuesday week, and with the new attraction of Miss Smith’s return to London, added to it’s own intrinsic merits, went off with much spirit and applause. It is a border story, full of the deadly hatreds of the Percy and the Douglas, and turns upon the common-place circumstance of a daughter compelled by her father to relinquish one lover and marry another; jealousy, of course, ensues on the part of the latter; the lady preserves her honour but cannot command her heart; and an innocent interview, which occurs between her and her first love, gives rise to proceedings of blind desperation, which ultimately involve the three parties in destruction, and leave the wretched father with all the weight of the moral upon his grey head. There are few features of originality in this story, and none at all in it’s characters; but the incidents succeed each other with a very simple and unobstructed prominence, so that the interest is sustained to the last; and at a time like the present, when the language of elegant writing is scarcely even attempted on the stage, or attempted only to be involuntarily burlesqued, the tragedy of Percy comes upon us with a great and attractive air of superiority, and would bear, I think, frequent repetition. Is it really true that the authoress made serious and devout protestations against the revival of this moral piece? If the reader can inform me with certainty on this point, I shall be happy to enter some counter protestations, in next week’s paper, against this religious piece of suicide and the feelings that would produce it. Miss Smith, who performed the heroine, is decidedly our best tragic actress next to Mrs. Siddons. Her face is intelligent, her eye fine, her voice clear and powerful, and she has evidently a perfect understanding of her author; but a perfect understanding of text and a perfect feeling of it's spirit, are things which Mr. Kemble has long shewn to be distinct, and it is not to be denied, that though Miss Smith stands next to Mrs. Siddons, there is as great an interval between them as between first rate genius and first rate declamation. The critic's opinion is unfortunately enabled to be more decisive on this head, and indeed to take a considerable step on the side of condemnation beyond what he formerly would have done, in as much as Miss Smith, during her absence, appears to have been indulged in her propensity for what is theatrical, to an extent that has seriously injured her: she is more of an attitudinarian than formerly; and her whole performance of Elwina was little better than a monotonous flow of well-read periods, interspersed with the white handkerchief, except in one or two instances where she shewed us what she could do by studying nature, particularly in the sobbing request she made her father not to kneel to her when she was dying,—a touch of pathos which admirably relieved the blankness of her despair. I sincerely hope that I shall have something better to record of this lady next week, for she has too much talent not to make us lament her errors; and if she will not do her best to console us for the approaching loss of Mrs. Siddons, who will?—Who can?
